steps.text: This lsass.exe registry write alert under a path containing '\RunTime\' looks like it could be a false positive, possibly just a substring match against '\Run'. I should pull the relation to check further.

arguments.reasoning: Read the registry write details (key path, value) by lsass.exe
Get the full registry key path to see if it is an autostart location
Check lsass.exe image path, user, and parent for legitimacy

steps.text: This registry key is W32Time SecureTimeLimits RunTime, which is Windows Secure Time Seeding — a normal lsass write and benign. I'm wondering if there's a separate accessed_process signal worth checking, possibly a credential dump against lsass, but the actual alert here concerns the registry write itself.

arguments.reasoning: Check whether some process accessed lsass suspiciously (credential dumping)

steps.text: SysMain accessing with 0x2000 is just standard Superfetch behavior — that's benign, so I'll classify it accordingly.

submission.reasoning: False positive from a substring match. The rule matched '\Run' inside '\RunTime\'. The write came from C:\windows\system32\lsass.exe on workstation5, which set the QWORD value HKLM\System\CurrentControlSet\Services\W32Time\SecureTimeLimits\RunTime\SecureTimeTickCount. This is Windows Time's Secure Time Seeding state that lsass updates as part of its normal work. It is not an autostart (Run/RunOnce) location. The only process that accessed lsass did so with minimal rights (0x2000), and its call trace runs through svchost/sysmain.dll, which is the SysMain service and normal. There is no sign of persistence or credential access.
